reviews.summary: Buys the racket after selling a Nox that was hard to control on the right side, and picks the Neuron 02 for its control. Calls the control excellent, with easy lobs, a comfortable swing and a good rebound. Finds power a little lower than the Vertex, so it suits control play more than attack. Notes a weight of 360, which feels light and easy to manoeuvre. Likes the orange vibration damping points and the 3D surface that helps spin. Adds an extra overgrip for a surer hold. Advises offensive players to look at the Vertex, Geo, Nox or Siux instead.
reviews.more: Sees the Neuron and Vertex as close, with the Neuron slightly better for control and the Vertex stronger. Explains that the Neuron 02 Edge has a more diamond shape, so it gives more attack and power, while this one is for control only. Chooses the new 2026 model so it lasts longer. Suggests changing the overgrip every three or four sessions, depending on how sweaty the hands are, and prefers white so dirt is easy to see. Likes perforated grips for comfort.

reviews.quote: Mi piace proprio il modo in cui si gestisce palla dal fondo.
reviews.summary: Tests the 2026 Neuron 02 on court and finds a welcoming racket with easy ball output, a medium sweet spot and a lot of spin. Weighs it at 369 g with a 25 cm balance and calls it very manoeuvrable. Rates it best from the back of the court, with smash in kick as a standout. Finds power limited compared with Vertex and Hack, and feel less direct than the Vertex. Rates sweet spot 8 minus, spin 8.5, comfort 8, power 7 and control 7.5. Calls the price high and gives value 5.5. Suits intermediate players, mostly right-handed, who want easy help.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Counter Viper, which is heavier, higher balanced and more complete for attack. Finds the Siux ST4 more powerful, while the Neuron has easier ball output, more control and handling. Notes the Exacore handle adds about 10 g, so it plays like roughly 360 g. Likes that the grip lace now exits the centre, so an aftermarket grip fits easily. Says value could reach 6.5 to 7 if the street price falls.

smash in kick as a standout

reviews.quote: se siente mucho más controlable a velocidades altas
reviews.summary: Compares the 2026 Neuron 02 with the Edge version on court at baseline, volley and overhead. Finds the standard version has a hybrid, more teardrop shape with a 250 mm balance, 365 g weight and a medium hard, dry feel. Rates it as the more controllable racket at high pace, with better manoeuvrability and a sweet spot about equal to the Edge. Notes the ball needs more arm to travel and the racket gives less power and ball exit. Says it feels closer to the 2025 Neuron. Suits players who want control and versatility, while those after power are pointed to the Edge.
reviews.more: Compares by situation: the standard version wins at the back of the court, the Edge wins at the net and overhead, and bandeja and víbora are close. Finds the Edge more powerful, with a 261 mm balance and a diamond shape. Notes both share 3K carbon, a multi-EVA rubber with softer outer layers, Prisma Lock and four Easy Vibes. Prefers the standard version on the víbora, as it allows full acceleration without losing control of the ball.
highlights: more controllable racket at high pace

reviews.creator: EverythingPadel
reviews.quote: It definitely works well in volley battles.
reviews.summary: Compares the 2026 Bullpadel range, with the normal Neuron described as a teardrop shape racket that is fairly well balanced between power and control. Finds a stiff 3K carbon build with a firm feel, but a lighter body at about 350 to 355 g, roughly 5 to 10 g lighter. Says the lower weight makes it more maneuverable and gives a faster swing at the net, so it works well in volley battles. Notes a textured surface with small bumps and lines for spin rather than sandpaper. Suggests it suits players who move quickly, play overheads fast and want a mix of power and control.
reviews.more: Places it in a lineup from most control to most power, after the Vertex Hybrid and Hack Hybrid and before Explode Comfort and the Neuron Edge. Calls the Neuron Edge a more powerful version with a wider geometric face, more head heavy and a little lighter. Links the Neuron style to Chingotto. Picks the Vertex Hybrid and Hack Hybrid as personal favourites instead, for their control.
highlights: fairly well balanced between power and control
textured surface with small bumps and lines

reviews.creator: El chini consejo
reviews.quote: es una pala muy polivalente, que va bastante bien
reviews.summary: Tests the racket after four days of play, describing a hybrid shape, 3D rough face and a medium low balance that does not feel head heavy. Finds the feel a notch firmer than medium and a touch softer than the Bullpadel Hack. Reports good ball exit that is not a trampoline, with strong results on lobs, wall exits, bandeja and vibora. Says good smash technique lets them bring balls back and even serve out. Recommends it to intermediate to advanced players, adding that beginners could adapt easily. Names the price as the only real downside. Calls it versatile, delivering in almost every area.
reviews.more: Compares the feel with last year's Nox 12K, which it resembles closely, and has not yet tried this year's version. Finds the bandeja and vibora much better than last year's Neuron and close to the model from two years ago, which they still prefer. Says the 3D rough face grips the ball slightly and that the exit is a little stronger than the model from two years ago. Notes the weight can be customised at the top of the frame.

reviews.creator: Extreme Padel
reviews.quote: le modèle Neuron classique, c'est un must de chez must
reviews.summary: Tests the classic Neuron 2026 in the lab and on court. Measures balance at 253 mm against 255 mm claimed, weight at 370 g without the wrist strap, rigidity at 65 and swingweight at 159.4, which points to a handy, very rigid racket. Reads a twist weight of 18.6 as stable on centred hits. Feels the manoeuvrability in defence, with easy low balls and precise lobs. Calls it excellent at the net for bandejas and viboras, with good length and real control. Notes a clear power gain over the previous version on smashes. Suits players of level 5 and above who build points and place the ball.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Neuron Edge, a diamond shape with balance at 256 mm, rigidity at 63 and swingweight at 162.2. Finds the Edge more punchy at the net and on smashes, with easier power. Prefers the Edge slightly for sharper viboras, yet calls the classic a must at the net. Notes the previous Neuron had a balance of 245 mm and was even more manoeuvrable.
highlights: easy low balls and precise lobs
clear power gain over the previous version

reviews.creator: Padel5
reviews.quote: Es ágil, estable y bastante permisiva
reviews.summary: Tests the 2026 Neuron 02 across volleys, bandeja, rulo to the fence, drop shots and defence. Calls it a control and precision racket, not an explosive one, but very reliable. Finds a firm, not soft feel that gives security on the volley and lets players place the ball and hold the net. Says the bandeja feels balanced and can be repeated without arm fatigue. Notes the rulo grips the ball enough for spin without it sticking. Finds the drop shot needs touch but responds. Rates defence as probably where it feels most comfortable, agile, stable and fairly forgiving. Suits players who build the point and defend well.

reviews.quote: I really like that control on the ball actually.
reviews.summary: Tests the Neuron 02 from the back and front of the court and finds great control, putting the ball where they want with volleys. Calls the weight and balance lovely, with a medium balance and 3K carbon. Notes a little more power than last year, though it has to be hit a little to get the power. Describes the new Neuron core working with Prism Lock to spread contact and add precision. Finds accuracy from the back of the court as well. Sees the Edge as the pick for more pop and aggressive play, thanks to its Geo shape.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Neuron 02 Edge, which has a Geo shape, a bigger surface area, slightly more head weight and more rebound. Finds the Edge gives more pop on volleys and overheads while keeping good precision. Notes both rackets share the Neuron core, Prism Lock and dampening technology. Says the Edge could suit aggressive players, and likes its mix of pop and accuracy for their own aggressive shots.

Notes a lower balance than the diamond shaped Edge, at 25.7 cm, so it moves faster on court while the Edge gives more power. Suggests it for attacking right side players who want an offensive racket that stays manoeuvrable.

reviews.quote: It is also still a very reactive racket
reviews.summary: Compares the HRD+ with the standard Metalbone 3.5 on each area of the court, using their own unit in standard screw configuration at 369 g and a 27 cm balance. Finds the High Memory rubber firmer, still very reactive, with a sweet spot the 3.5 beats by about 15%. Prefers it for blocks and bandeja play because the extra firmness gives more control over speeds. Finds smashes easy for power, but calls it more demanding, with a higher ceiling for players who swing fast. Rates handling as limited because of the long handle and added weight. Picks it over the 3.5 overall.
reviews.more: Finds the standard 3.5 easier, with a larger sweet spot, a fuller sound and earlier power for slower swings. Calls the 3.5 more reactive than a Vertex and the HRD+ livelier than the Viper range. Measures 355 g and 26.8 cm balance with all screws removed, and would remove them to improve handling at a small cost in power.
highlights: higher ceiling for players who swing fast

reviews.creator: Tom Pandore - Padel
reviews.quote: pour le smash, vraiment impeccable, ça smashe très très fort
reviews.summary: Tests it in one-on-one drills covering volleys, back of court, vibora and smash, then reports how it felt in matches. Finds it an attacking racket with head-heavy balance, 360 g on their sample, and clearly harder to manoeuvre than the standard Metalbone. Finds the sweet spot easy to hit and the feel softer than expected. Notes that well-timed volleys and smashes go out very hard, but fast balls leave them late and reflex volleys come out average. Says it rewards raw power over assisted power. Recommends it for aggressive attackers with strong technique and a racket sport background, and warns that players lacking that may regress in defence.
reviews.more: Compares the handling with the standard Metalbone and the previous HRD versions, and finds this one heavier in the hand. Notes that the screws can be removed to change weight without shifting the balance much. Finds the vibora benefits from the weight when relaxed, giving heavy deep balls, but quick flat bandeja shots expose the handling. Says the ball does not rise high over the net from the back of the court. Reports feeling late on most balls in real matches.
highlights: harder to manoeuvre than the standard Metalbone
rewards raw power over assisted power

reviews.creator: Simone Mazzola Padel
reviews.quote: potenza totale con controllo, ma solo se sei allenato
reviews.summary: Plays three matches on both sides of the court, and feels it may be the best Metalbone Hard so far. Finds defence better than expected, with reliable lobs and a good sweet spot that forgives off-centre hits. Calls the attacking power heavy and fast, and feels the arm shock clearly lower than on the 2025 model, though the racket stays stiff and demanding. Says it suits advanced left side players with technique and physique, not beginners, classic intermediates or players worried about elbows. Warns against buying it for the name alone, and advises testing it over several consecutive matches.
reviews.more: Compares it with the 2025 model, finding it noticeably less punishing on the arm. Notes the price is hard to justify, but buying with a discount code may make sense. Lists three buying mistakes: expecting it to make a player more offensive, judging it after half an hour, and ignoring the court side played. Fits the left side best, and is not the first choice for someone who only plays on the right.

reliable lobs and a good sweet spot

reviews.creator: padelwithmax (Padel Deals test)
reviews.quote: you really can drive your shots with great power and precision
reviews.summary: Tests the 2026 Metalbone HRD+ across the back of the court, volleys, viboras and kick smashes. Finds the harder foam makes it feel firmer than the standard Metalbone and less maneuverable than the Metalbone Control, though the sweet spot stays quite big. Gets great power when timing the ball well, even from the back, with great control and precision. Likes the zippy, punchy volleys that reward good timing. Struggles to get the diamond shape through the air fast enough on viboras, but the ball flies when it works. Calls it a racket for advanced attacking players who want to dominate with power, and rates it 8.8 out of 10.

reviews.creator: Extreme Padel
reviews.quote: C'est vraiment une arme de destruction massive réservée à des joueurs vraiment avancés
reviews.summary: Tests the HRD+ on court after measuring it with the weights removed, then refitting them in the centre of the frame. Measures 369 g with a 275 mm balance and a 13.5 cm handle, and calls it very tiring. Finds it even more demanding than the standard Metalbone, with no forgiveness on off-centre hits and a little less touch from the dense High Memory foam. Rates it very powerful, with surgical precision on volley blocks and easy smashes. Gives 64 for comfort and 64 for tolerance. Recommends it only to advanced players with strong technique and a strong arm, and advises against it for anyone with arm pain.
reviews.more: Compares it with the standard Metalbone, which has a softer foam, 72 for comfort, 71 for tolerance and 82 for ball exit. Finds the standard version more versatile and easier on the arm. Describes the HRD+ at the net as demanding, needing good timing and a big arm, while the standard model lets the ball escape too easily on volleys. Calls the HRD+ smash a cheat code that sends balls out with little effort.

reviews.creator: Super Padel Bros
reviews.quote: Per quanto mi riguarda è una pala stupenda.
reviews.summary: Tests it from the baseline, at the net and on overhead shots, finding it slightly less hard than the 2025 model with a slightly wider but still severe sweet spot. Rates volleys nine, viper and bandeja nine and a half, and smash ten. Finds the touch dry and honest, blocks very stable, and spin good but not spectacular. Calls comfort good, since the vibration problem of older Metalbone models was fixed from 2025. Weighs 346 g without the extra weights and prefers it that way. Recommends it for advanced intermediate players and up, who need a firm arm and fast ball speed.
reviews.more: Notes the weight system adds about 11 g with all weights fitted but shifts the balance only slightly, so prefers it without them. Advises leaving the plastic screws in the head if no weights are fitted, to stop sand entering the frame. Finds defence harder when opponents press at the net, since the racket gives no free ball exit. Criticises the leash, which has no wrist pad, and calls the included wrist band uncomfortable. Struggles on soft balls scooped from below without stepping forward.

reviews.creator: Otro Nivel Padel / Justpadel
reviews.quote: for some reason fibra was amazing
reviews.summary: Tests the Metalbone Hard against the Metalbone Control and the normal Metalbone on court in defence, volleys and smashes. Finds it much harder and heavier than the others, with less trampoline feel, so timing must be on point and late players will struggle. Calls it very powerful if the whole arm is used, but hard for wrist players. Rates the vibora and the kick smash best of the three, with the ball bouncing highest on the smash. Gives 8.9 out of 10 and rates it above the Bullpadel Vertex for being lighter. Advises beginners and medium players to avoid it, and suggests it only for strong pro level players.
reviews.more: Compares it to the Babolat Viper Juan Lebron, finding more touch than that racket, more power than the Bullpadel Vertex and a ball that goes deeper into the racket than the Vertex. Finds it harder than Nox diamond rackets, with slightly less touch. Likes that it is not heavy for a diamond racket. Recommends the Metalbone Control for intermediate players and the normal Metalbone for high intermediate players. Suggests players who smash a lot choose the Metalbone or Metalbone Hard.
highlights: much harder and heavier than the others
very powerful if the whole arm is used
reviews.short: Tests the Metalbone Hard against the Metalbone Control and the normal Metalbone on court in defence, volleys and smashes. reviews.creator: Padel Test by Roberto Cardi
reviews.quote: Davvero la seria candidata a essere la numero uno per lo Smash.
reviews.summary: Tests it on court shot by shot, covering volleys, smashes, bandejas, vibora and wall exits, and gives a 10 for each. Finds the power outstanding and the sweet spot wide, rounded and higher than last year, reaching the second row of holes. Plays it with the 11.2 g weights on a 350 g racket, about 365 g total, and thinks it would play even better without them. Calls the feel slightly firm but comfortable, with a little more comfort than the 2025. Sees possible arm vibrations from the aluminium plates in hot weather, but is not certain. Suits advanced intermediate players up to professionals.
reviews.more: Describes a diamond shape with carbon 16K faces and high density EVA. Prefers it to the standard Metalbone 2026 for aggressive players, calling the standard model more versatile and better for less aggressive play. Notes the HRD gives less free ball exit on blocks than the standard version. Advises removing the weights for more maneuverability and less load on the arm.
highlights: reaching the second row of holes
a little more comfort than the 2025

reviews.creator: Dani 13
reviews.quote: es una pala que realmente no te permite mucho fallo
reviews.summary: Tests the 2026 model across defence, mid-court, volley and smash. Describes it as medium-hard, about 7.5 to 8 out of 10 in hardness, yet more reactive than similar rackets. Finds smash and bandeja the strongest areas, with easy power from the high balance and long handle. Calls it one of the most powerful rackets at this hardness. Struggles most in defence and volley, where the head-heavy balance slows movement and the ball can float to the glass. Notes a clear gap between sweet spot and off-centre hits. Recommends it for backhand players of medium level or above.
reviews.more: Compares it with the 2025 model and finds the feel very similar, so the extra cost is not worth it unless the rope-style cord or the looks matter. Says the 2025 is much cheaper. Finds the standard Metalbone a little more forgiving at medium hardness. Notes the screws add about 12 g and move the balance from 26.7 to 27 cm.

most powerful rackets at this hardness
gap between sweet spot and off-centre hits

reviews.creator: Padel Review
reviews.quote: una racchetta offensiva, molto aggressiva, però è molto tecnica anche
reviews.summary: Tests the racket without the weights, where it measures 356 g and balances at 27.8 cm, and likes it that way. Finds a hard, diamond shaped racket with a small sweet spot that demands precision, but one that lets players swing fully from the back without the ball flying long. Rates spin as very good, with no vibration, and sees it as most at home at the net and on smashes. Calls it technical and offensive, suited to intermediate high to advanced players, mainly on the left. Gives 6 out of 10 for value.
reviews.more: Notes that adding the weights gives 368 g and a balance of 27.6 cm, which they see as useful for weight more than balance. Finds it better without the weights overall, and keeps the small rubber plugs in place to stop sand entering the frame. Sees the 2026 model as very close to last year, with a longer cord replacing the strap and a feel that may be slightly less hard.
highlights: most at home at the net

reviews.creator: Padel5
reviews.quote: On smashes, it goes like a cannon.
reviews.summary: Calls it the most powerful racket in the new Wilson line, with a diamond shape and high balance made for attacking players. Finds smashes go like a cannon when the sweet spot is hit, helped by the 15K carbon and firm feel. Rates bandeja and vibora responses as very good, with plenty of spin and depth from the rough texture. Finds volleys solid if hit decisively, but says it does not forgive a slow arm. Notes it is less clumsy at the back than a head-heavy racket might be, while drop shots need extra finesse. Recommends it to offensive, mid-to-high or advanced level players.
reviews.more: Describes the hole pattern as helping control and spin, so defending is possible with some comfort, though not its main strength. Says spin shots to the side fence come off easily thanks to the texture and the carbon control on lifted shots. Finds it not the most sensitive racket, yet players with good touch can still get a lot out of it. Suggests it suits players who want to push up top without losing all control at the back.

does not forgive a slow arm

reviews.creator: Mejora Tu Padel
reviews.quote: This is not for all audiences, a logically more offensive and more refined shovel
reviews.summary: Tests the Pro against the regular Defy and the LS, with a second player giving input. Records 366 g without string and a 260 mm balance, and finds the touch softer than normal but the blade more solid. Notes more sweet spot than the LS, even on hits near the tip. Feels the ball rise in defense because of the tip-heavy balance, though it adds power from above. Calls it a more offensive, refined racket that is not for all audiences. Rates price-quality at five or six because prices are high. Names the roughness, sandpaper and 3D effect as pros, and little difference from the regular Defy as a con.
reviews.more: Finds the regular Defy a point of balance between the two, more homogeneous, with less power than the Pro. Hears a harder sound on the regular Defy than on the LS, and calls the LS drivable for players with less experience. Reports the second player liked the Pro most but would pick the regular Defy to avoid trouble. Would play the Pro for extra power if able to hold it, otherwise the regular one. Would prefer the string centered rather than to the side.

little difference from the regular Defy

reviews.quote: grande la manovrabilità quando vado a fare l'uscita di parete alta
reviews.summary: Tests the diamond-shaped racket on court and scores each shot: 9.5 for volleys, high shots, basic shots and the low wall exit, 9 for the high wall exit, 8.5 for blocks, 10 for the smash and 6 for price. Finds great manoeuvrability, perfect cuts and no arm discomfort. Calls the sweet spot centre-high and fairly wide. Notes power is good but not maximum. Finds blocks good but without a sense of extreme stability. Rates it for advanced intermediate players up to experts and professionals. Expects it to be one of the best sellers of 2025.
reviews.more: Describes it as the first diamond racket from Wilson, following the teardrop Blade Pro. Notes 15K carbon faces with a visible 3D texture, a honeycomb surface for spin, medium hardness Power foam and a bridge meant to reduce vibration reaching the handle. Gives a 6 for the price and says Wilson is starting to win them over with a pro racket at this price.

reviews.creator: El chini consejo
reviews.quote: Me gusta mucho la pala desde aquí, desde el fondo de pista.
reviews.summary: Tests the diamond shaped, rough faced racket over a first part covering baseline and volleys, with a player who has used it for two weeks and plays up to three times a day. Weighs it at 377 g with a 26.1 balance after swapping the original grip for two overgrips. Goes in expecting a less manageable, harder racket but finds it comfortable and very manageable, with a medium hard feel. Notes that ball exit is controlled rather than reactive, so lobs need a longer swing. Finds it strong when pushing volleys, and the rough surface grips the ball well for spin. Leaves bandeja, vibora and smashes for part two.
reviews.more: Compares it with the standard version, noting a different carbon grade, and finds lobs easier to feel on the other one. Rates the feel less dry than a Babolat Viper, which seems a bit more rigid. Calls it close to the Adidas Metalbone HRD 2024 in feel and sound, though with a longer handle. Takes off the original grip and uses two thin overgrips to feel the racket more.

reviews.quote: Truly fantastic spin, on par with the top of the category
reviews.summary: Tests the Wilson Defy Pro V1 on court as a diamond shaped attacking racket with 15K carbon faces, a rough Spin Texture surface and Power Foam. Finds it powerful but less extreme than the specs suggest, because the balance is medium rather than very high. Praises the spin as top of the category, the solid loud sound on every hit and the great play at the net. Notes weak ball output on lobs and baseline shots, and a sweet spot that is decent but not wide. Sees it as a left side racket, though workable on the right for strong players who like finishing points.
reviews.more: Finds the handle very comfortable out of the box, with no overgrip needed, and the wrist strap good though it twists now and then. Gives 9 for power, 8.5 for control, 8 for maneuverability, 6.5 for ball output, 7.5 for sweet spot and 8.2 as the average. Finds the mirror in the box a bit much.

reviews.creator: Padel Review
reviews.quote: what surprised me the most is the control that it has
reviews.summary: Tests it with a sparring partner in baseline, net and overhead drills, then a short match challenge. Finds the spin texture devastating and the effects top of the category. Calls the control excellent, the thing that surprised them most. Expects more power, especially on the flat smash, though finds it still powerful and very good for the kick. Weighs a 366 gram sample with a medium balance, which adds handling but costs a little pure power. Calls the sweet spot good, with little ball exit on short blocks. Suits intermediate players, mainly left side, though aggressive right side players should try it. Gives price to quality a 7.
reviews.more: Compares the power foam with the Head version and finds Head more explosive, while this one feels stiffer. Rates it better than the Blade Pro and the Top Ten. Describes a diamond shape, 15K carbon faces, an intermediate hard touch and a comfortable handle that is perhaps slightly longer, with no overgrip. Warns that it gives little ball exit at the net on low balls, so players risk being attacked. Finds it short on deep flat shots when the arm movement is small, and says shoulder movement must be right.

reviews.creator: the4Set
reviews.quote: if you accelerate your arm even a little, the energy transfer is total.
reviews.summary: Tests the new Defy Pro, mostly with the factory grip removed, and compares it with the Defy and Defy LS. Finds it a diamond-shaped racket that moves well despite a high balance, with a large sweet spot and not much ball output. Notes that the rubber and carbon combination is very reactive, so hitting hard or accelerating the arm gives total energy transfer. Finds the 3D and sandy texture among the roughest they have felt, which at first slowed sliced volleys too much. Struggles to feel the ball on lobs and to control speed on bandejas. Rates it for players wanting a diamond racket that moves well and gives a ton of acceleration.
reviews.more: Lists the Defy Pro at 370 grams and 15K carbon, against the Defy at 365 grams and 3K carbon, and the LS at 355 grams and fiberglass. Finds the Pro the hardest of the three, though none feel very hard. Calls the grip long at 13 cm but thick from the factory. Feels the Blade V3 is as powerful or more on smashes, but gets better results from the Defy Pro because it swings faster.

reviews.creator: Probando Palas
reviews.summary: Tests the racket on the court at the back, net and in aerial play after reviewing the specs. Finds a medium-hard, reactive feel despite the soft name, with 365 g stock weight, 368 g in their setup and a balance close to 280 mm. Calls it manageable for a power racket and better optimised on off-centre hits than the standard Viper, though the sweet spot is only average. Rates volleys, blocking and the vibora very highly, while the bandeja needs a faster hand and the fence-bound smash takes more work. Says it suits players who want power but need a little extra help.
reviews.more: Compares it with the standard Juan Lebron Viper, finding it less rigid, easier on off-centre hits and more playable for smashing out of bounds, though not as strong there. Notes the 3D texture adds a little more spin than previous editions, where the ball slid more. Finds the drop shot and short volleys need a good touch and more wrist. Prefers round shapes for smashing, which explains some trouble with the fence-bound smash. Plans to keep playing it for at least a few matches.

reviews.quote: es la pala que más me ha gustado de esta línea del lobo

Rates the hardness at about 8.5 out of 10 despite the Soft name, with a dry feel and an average weight of 365 g. Finds it more comfortable, easier to handle and with a slightly better sweet spot than the Viper, though the ball dies when hit off centre. Gets good feeling on eight of ten smashes, against five with the Viper. Ranks the víbora and bandeja zone first, then smash, defence and volley. Suits players with a good technical level who want feel over help.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Verón, which feels softer, more reactive and more helpful but gives less feel and control. Finds it slightly better than the Technical models thanks to a drier touch. Notes a rounded end cap that does not dig in with little overgrip. Says it suits players who want power without a very bouncy racket such as the Adidas Metalbone Hard. Finds the volley the weakest zone, since short balls come out when blocking without following through.

Struggles to notice a very different feel between the 3.0 and the 3.0 Soft. Notes the Soft feels more flexible, but not by a big margin. Says that for a soft model it does not feel soft and calls it a hard racket. Recommends trying it first, because it may suit a player or may not, and another Babolat model could fit their game better. Reminds that it is a slightly hard racket.

reviews.quote: Una cosa strepitosa come gioco il pallonetto con questa pala.
reviews.summary: Tests it on court and scores each shot separately. Gives 10 for the volley, 9 for the high ball, 10 for the low wall exit, 9 for the high wall exit, 8.5 for the block and 8 for the smash. Finds plenty of power, a good but not very wide sweet spot and a hard feel, rated 7 for hardness. Calls manoeuvrability limited, needing a stronger arm. Gives 5.5 for value. Recommends it to advanced players who hit flat and cut less, not to intermediates or players with a thin arm.
reviews.more: Says it is harder than the name suggests, softer than the Viper Technical 3.0 but less soft than many other rackets. Reports that some sponsored players moved from the Technical to the Soft. Finds it excels at lobs and touch play. Expected more power and manoeuvrability on the smash. Describes the sweet spot as a half circle starting near the end of the A in the Babolat logo.

reviews.creator: Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel
reviews.quote: La Viper soft no se queda corta en absoluto
reviews.summary: Compares the 2026 Viper Soft 3.0 head to head with the regular Viper 3.0 in defence, volley, bandeja and smash. Finds it is not soft at all, rating the hardness as medium hard, only slightly more forgiving than the regular version. Measures a balance of 26.6 cm on their unit and notes 365 g average weight, plus or minus 10 g. Picks it for defence thanks to a slightly bigger sweet spot and better low speed ball exit. Calls volleys and bandeja a tie. Gives the smash to the regular Viper, which feels more explosive at top speed. Says it suits experienced players, and that none of these rackets is easy.
reviews.more: Describes the regular Viper as harder, with a carbon plate inside the foam, while the Soft uses Soft Carbon and a classic black EVA core. Notes both sound metallic and sharp on the bandeja. Finds the extra balance on the Soft helps push the head forward and add depth. Says the regular version gives a bit more at maximum speed. Recommends the Soft for a more docile contact without losing a dry feel.
highlights: Calls volleys and bandeja a tie

reviews.trade: Less explosive in smashes and still demanding, not easy to use.

reviews.creator: pdhsports
reviews.quote: it's great on the power, really good on the volleys
reviews.summary: Tests the new Viper Soft on court alongside the rest of the 2026 Technical range. Finds the different carbon plating gives a much softer feel than the older, firm Technical, while the power stays high. Notes good reaction on volleys and says off-centred hits do not travel as far but no longer feel firm. Says the softness makes defence easier, though the racket is still head heavy. Calls it very forgiving for a diamond shaped racket and rates it for intermediate and advanced players. Says they loved the new plated carbon.
reviews.more: Compares it with the standard Viper, which feels firmer and demands more work in defence, and needs the sweet spot for power. Says earlier Technical rackets had a small sweet spot and a firm feel, and the Viper Soft keeps the power and new shape while softening the response. Describes the sound as going off like a rocket even in the soft version. Rates the standard Viper for intermediate and advanced players.
highlights: very forgiving for a diamond shaped racket

reviews.keyPoint: Soft carbon plating keeps the power of the Technical.
reviews.stood: Much softer feel with the power kept and forgiving off-centre hits.
reviews.trade: Still head heavy, and off-centre hits do not travel as far.

reviews.creator: Setup Padel | Mario Pazos
reviews.quote: me encanta el tacto que tiene
reviews.summary: Tests it on court through winter temperatures and calls the ball exit excellent and predictable, with no surprises wherever the ball is hit. Finds a medium-hard, dry feel that is firmer in cold weather at 6 to 7 degrees, closer to the regular Viper, and ideal around 15 degrees. Rates the sweet spot as standard and high on the face. Calls the handling spectacular for an offensive racket at 366 g, about 10 g lighter than the regular Viper. Places the power one step below the regular Viper. Recommends it to intermediate-high and advanced offensive players, not to those moving up from basic intermediate. Bought it and keeps it as their current racket.
reviews.more: Places the power between the Neuron Edge and another offensive racket tried recently, and above most offensive options played this year. Sees it as a step for players leaving a hybrid racket for the offensive shape without a very demanding racket. Doubts it suits defensive players who play tactically. Wonders whether it turns bouncier when the weather warms. Notes the Black EVA rubber and a 3D rough surface, more marked than other rackets but not exaggerated.
highlights: handling spectacular for an offensive racket

reviews.keyPoint: Offensive racket with handling that suits amateur players.
reviews.stood: Predictable ball exit and very easy handling for an offensive racket at 366 g.
reviews.trade: Firmer in cold weather and a standard sweet spot with little forgiveness.

reviews.creator: Nmscontrolpadel
reviews.quote: siendo de potencia se siente muy bien la bola
reviews.summary: Tests the new Viper Soft at 360 grams with a high balance of about 27 centimetres, and finds it handles well despite a slight head-heavy feel. Notes a diamond shape that is less pronounced, a 3D rough surface with gloss finish and a hard, dry touch. Feels a little more sweet spot and ball exit than the normal Viper, and calls it closer to a Viper that already has some use. Calls it very complete, with plenty of control among the most powerful rackets. Rates it for advanced players who want power and ball control. Warns that the shape and dry touch must suit, and that slower rhythm needs a push.
reviews.more: Notes the cord is not interchangeable this year but is comfortable, with a round end cap and a grip of standard size or slightly more, shorter than usual Babolat models. Finds it controlled at high rhythm, since the ball does not fly out despite the reactivity. Says short strokes and half volleys still get good ball exit. Points to the pronounced three-band bridge as a help for handling. Finds it picks up spin well despite the gloss 3D finish.
highlights: handles well despite a slight head-heavy feel

reviews.keyPoint: Complete power racket that still handles well.
reviews.stood: Combines power with good handling and ball feel for advanced players.
reviews.trade: Needs an advanced level and a liking for the dry touch and shape.

reviews.creator: the4Set
reviews.quote: It has more ball output, so you can generate faster shots with less effort.
reviews.summary: Tests the Soft version against the standard Viper Juan Lebron 3.0 2026 with a unit weighing 362 g and a balance of 26.8 cm. Finds it medium to hard rather than truly soft, with a bigger sweet spot, more ball output and easier acceleration. Rates it a little better to move than the hard version, though not maneuverable, and more comfortable in defense. Notes worse control at high speed and on volleys. Smashes 10 balls with each racket and sees similar results, with a slight edge for the hard one. Suggests it for offensive players who want a lot of speed without much effort.
reviews.more: Compares it with the standard version, which has more control and power but demands good physical condition and suits warmer places. Says the soft model suits colder places, since heat softens it too much. Explains that it uses 3K twill carbon and a lower hardness core, and that the real difference comes from the core. Finds the roughness does not grab the ball enough on either racket.
reviews.short: Tests the Soft version against the standard Viper Juan Lebron 3.0 2026 with a unit weighing 362 g and a balance of 26.8 cm. reviews.keyPoint: Softer, easier Viper for offensive players with less strength.
reviews.stood: Bigger sweet spot and more ball output give speed with less effort.
reviews.trade: Less control at high speed and on volleys than the hard version.

reviews.creator: Mejora Tu Padel
reviews.quote: Esta es una pala exigente, es una pala dura
reviews.summary: Tests it for two weeks in Madrid, Tenerife and Rome, in heat, humidity and cold. Measures 369 g without strings and a balance of 252 mm, yet finds it feels heavier and more head-heavy than the numbers suggest. Rates it as a hard, demanding racket that is spectacular in attack. Struggles in transition play and counterattack, where low volleys float and go up. Warns that it is tough in winter, not for players with elbow problems or limited skill. Recommends it only for those who want a hard racket with balance, and prefers the Counter Viper for their own game.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Technical Viper, which has a rounder shape and is easier to handle and defend with. Notes that glossy and 3D finishes feel slightly harder than matte ones. Lists 3K carbon with a hard EVA core, so it is firm on paper. Compares it with the Siux Phenix Pro, similar in balance but harder. Calls the Counter Viper a better fit for them.
highlights: not for players with elbow problems

reviews.keyPoint: Hard, head-heavy attacking racket that punishes transition play.
reviews.stood: Spectacular in attack and works well in heat and humidity.
reviews.trade: Punishes transition play and counterattack, and is too hard for elbow problems.
reviews.compared: Babolat Technical Viper, Babolat Counter Viper, Siux Phenix Pro

reviews.creator: Padel-Point
reviews.quote: it's all about power with this racket
reviews.summary: Presents the Viper Juan Lebron 3.0 as the heaviest racket of the Babolat Juan Lebron series at 370 g, with a shiny finish, diamond shape, head heavy balance and the sweet spot at the top. Calls it all about power, with hard foam, good for smashes and fast balls. Warns it is not for beginners and is tough to handle, needing a good hand and good control, otherwise little power is generated. Notes the arm gets heavier after one hour of defending off the glass. Recommends it as a great racket for experienced and advanced players who want to play like Juan Lebron.
reviews.more: Compares it within the series: the Veron is the lightest at about 360 g with carbon flex, and is maybe the most forgiving and easiest to handle. Finds the Viper Juan Lebron Soft sits between the Viper and the Veron at about 365 g, with softer foam that gives a bit more control while still generating power. Thinks more players can handle the Soft than the Viper 3.0, which they pick as the one to test for pure power.
highlights: great racket for experienced and advanced players

reviews.keyPoint: Heavy power racket for advanced players only.
reviews.stood: Huge power for smashes and fast balls, built for attacking play.
reviews.trade: Tough to handle at 370 g, and the arm tires after an hour.
reviews.compared: Babolat Viper Juan Lebron Soft, Babolat Veron Juan Lebron

reviews.creator: Justpadel
reviews.quote: So for those players that like to play hard, this is your racket.
reviews.summary: Calls it a powerful, hard racket built from 3K carbon, heavy and stiff. Finds it great for players who attack directly, lob, go to the net and block. Loses a little control when playing really fast. Finds it gives real power on smashes. Dislikes the hard touch personally, since they prefer softer rackets, though knows many players like it. Points softer players to the Soft version of the Lebron. Recommends it only for pro level players because the inside is quite hard and powerful. Rates it 7.1 out of 10.
highlights: powerful, hard racket built from 3K carbon

reviews.stood: Strong power for direct play, lobs, net play and blocking.
reviews.trade: Hard touch and some lost control at speed, only suits pro level players.

reviews.creator: Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel
reviews.quote: Si te pilla bien plantado y le pegas con todo, la Viper normal gana.
reviews.summary: Compares the 2026 Technical Viper 3.0 with the Soft version in defence, volley, bandeja and smash. Weighs their unit at 368 g with 26.2 cm of balance. Finds the hardness very high, above medium hard, with a small sweet spot that punishes off-centre hits. Notes a dry touch and medium maneuverability, with extra explosiveness appearing when swinging hard, which they think may come from the new carbon plate inside the foam. Gives it the smash point for more power and a firmer impact. Calls it a demanding racket for players with good physical condition, though a professional could use it.
reviews.more: Prefers the Soft version in defence, where it gives a little more help at low speed. Rates volleys as a tie, with the standard Viper more reactive on very offensive shots. Finds the bandeja level too, though the standard one gives a bit more at top speed. Notes 3K carbon on the last layer. Recommends it for players who can push at low speed and handle a racket 5 g heavier on average.
highlights: small sweet spot that punishes off-centre hits
extra explosiveness appearing when swinging hard
more power and a firmer impact

reviews.stood: More power and explosiveness than the Soft version in smashes and fast offensive shots.
reviews.trade: Very hard and demanding, with a small sweet spot and a dry touch.
reviews.compared: Babolat Technical Viper Soft 3.0, Head Extreme Pro

reviews.creator: PADELREVIEW ENG
reviews.quote: When you accelerate properly and hit the sweet spot, the power is massive.
reviews.summary: Tests the 2026 racket from the baseline, at the net and on overheads, then plays a match and gives scores per shot. Finds it stiff, explosive and very demanding, with massive power when the sweet spot is hit and little help if technique is poor. Calls it more reactive than the previous version but easier than the very first Technical Viper. Notes a weight of 378 g and a balance of 27 cm, which makes it hard to handle. Finds the volleys sharp and aggressive, the smashes penetrating and the rough face producing incredible spin. Recommends it for advanced left side players who like power.
reviews.more: Lists a diamond shape, 3K carbon where last year used 12K, a more reactive carbon power layer and a dynamic stability system. Likes the longer standard size handle and the comfortable wristband. Accepts the price because the racket is completely redesigned. Says arm training and technique are needed to manage the weight. Plays a short match with a partner before reading out scores per shot.
highlights: massive power when the sweet spot is hit

reviews.keyPoint: Powerful but demanding racket for advanced left side players.
reviews.stood: Massive power and strong spin on smashes and bibora.
reviews.trade: Demanding weight and balance, unforgiving without clean technique.

reviews.creator: Dani 13
reviews.quote: Es una pala que se controla muy bien en ritmos más rápidos
reviews.summary: Tests the 2026 Viper Juan Lebron with the same 3K carbon and hard rubber as last year, and finds a hard, technical, physical racket. Rates power as good and control as very good, with little rebound, and says it works best at faster rhythms. Notes it absorbs nothing and asks the player to push hard for the ball to travel. Finds the sweet spot smaller and the racket demanding for players not used to hard rackets. Warns about the 370 g weight and the 26.8 cm balance, which make it harder to handle.
reviews.more: Contrasts its low rebound with rackets that offer more, which help the ball run at lower effort. Says it suits players who like a hard feel and want the result to depend on their own push. Calls it technical and more demanding than other models, as the previous year's version was. Suggests it needs some adaptation before it feels good on court. Says the extra weight makes it less easy to manage than other options.
highlights: push hard for the ball to travel
reviews.short: Tests the 2026 Viper Juan Lebron with the same 3K carbon and hard rubber as last year, and finds a hard, technical, physical racket. reviews.keyPoint: Hard, technical racket that rewards players who push.
reviews.stood: Very good control and decent power at faster rhythms.
reviews.trade: Heavy, high balance, small sweet spot and little help for the ball.

reviews.creator: the4Set
reviews.quote: it's excellent if you have good technique and physical condition
reviews.summary: Tests the hard Viper Juan Lebron 2026 against its Soft sibling, using a unit of 366 g with a 27 cm balance. Finds it a hard racket with very little ball output, high control and a smaller sweet spot than the Soft. Rates the net game as the best part, since clean contact sends all the energy into the ball, and calls the smash impressive. Finds it heavy and hard to move in defense, and says the roughness could be much better. Recommends it for players with very good physical condition and technique who want a bit more power than control.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Soft version, which is 5 g lighter and uses 3K twill carbon and a softer core. Finds the Soft gives a bigger sweet spot, more ball output and easier handling, but less control. Says the hard version suits warm places, while the Soft suits cold ones. Tests 10 smashes with each racket and gets very similar results, with a slight win for the hard one. Notes the design is now electric orange, with the important parts unchanged from last year.
highlights: clean contact sends all the energy
very good physical condition and technique

reviews.keyPoint: Hard, controlled attacking racket for fit and technical players.
reviews.stood: Control and precise placement at the net, plus heavy smashes.
reviews.trade: Heavy and demanding, hard to move for players with limited fitness.

reviews.creator: Nico Ballesteros
reviews.summary: Compares the hybrid and attack versions of the Ventus 2026 side by side with a partner who has played the racket for a while, scoring aesthetics, shape, balance, hardness, sweet spot, control and power. Finds the hybrid teardrop shape very manageable and comfortable from the back of the court, and not much of a loss at the net. Rates the sweet spot of the hybrid as huge. Notes both rackets share 12K carbon, a MLD Black Eva core and Dual Spin surface, with a medium-firm feel and practically the same hardness. Gives power to the attack version, and suggests the hybrid suits versatile players who do not attack every ball.
reviews.more: Prefers the attack version's higher balance for extra power when attacking, even if less manageable, and says the hand compensates. Calls the hybrid more forgiving for players whose technique is less polished, while the attack version asks for a more technical player. Stresses that neither racket is better, only a better fit for each player, and advises testing or renting before buying.
highlights: sweet spot of the hybrid as huge
versatile players who do not attack every ball

reviews.keyPoint: Manageable hybrid shape with a huge sweet spot.
reviews.stood: Very manageable and comfortable from the back, with a huge sweet spot.
reviews.trade: Less power than the attack version and less suited to players who attack constantly.

reviews.creator: Canary Padel
reviews.quote: Una pala que tiene mucho control y mucha manejabilidad.
reviews.summary: Tests it on court in defence, volley, bandeja and vibora, and smash, plus a look at the design and technology. Finds a medium-hard, dry feel that is clearly harder than last year's 12K, with a medium balance and a medium weight that make it very easy to handle. Rates control as its standout trait, with the ball leaving the face predictably. Notes the rough surface grips spin well. Finds a little missing head balance for smashes and a little missing weight in the tip on volleys. Says it suits defensive players who want control and consistent feel rather than aggressive hitters.
reviews.more: Describes the red finish, the reworked tunnel with side gills, Black EVA double density foam and a 12K carbon that differs from last year. Notes it lacks the weight system of the AT10. Finds the gills help grip the handle. Hits off-centre and feels it a little stiffer, with the ball running less. Needs a slightly longer swing on volleys for depth. Thinks it could be one of the best selling Nox rackets this year and would pick it from the range.
reviews.short: Tests it on court in defence, volley, bandeja and vibora, and smash, plus a look at the design and technology. Finds a little missing head balance for smashes and a little missing weight in the tip on volleys. Says it suits defensive players who want control and consistent feel rather than aggressive hitters.
reviews.keyPoint: Very manageable control racket with a dry, medium-hard feel.
reviews.stood: Control and handling, with a dry feel that makes the ball predictable.
reviews.trade: Lacks a little weight and head balance for aggressive smashing.

reviews.creator: Extreme Padel
reviews.quote: Son gros point fort, c'est la tolérance et le contrôle.
reviews.summary: Tests the hybrid version of the Ventus range in the lab and on court, and measures 361.7 g, a low to medium balance of 247 mm, 62 RA stiffness and a swingweight of 155.2. Finds it very manoeuvrable with a good touch in defence, with great control for placed play at the net, and very tolerant on bandejas and vibora. Notes it lacks a little reactivity and length unless the arm and legs commit fully. Finds smashes hard to send out by three. Suggests it for intermediate to advanced players who like control and placement.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Genius 12K 2025 and finds it less powerful and less reactive, but far more manoeuvrable. Says control and tolerance are similar to the Genius 12K Light 2026, with similar power. Notes that the red hybrid has less inertia than the blue attack version, so it asks for more arm and leg engagement on length. Describes the attack version as more rigid, heavier in the head and less tolerant, aimed at advanced players. Mentions the hybrid is a teardrop shape with a standard 12.5 handle.
highlights: very manoeuvrable with a good touch
very tolerant on bandejas and vibora
lacks a little reactivity and length

reviews.stood: Very manoeuvrable, with great tolerance and control for placed play.
reviews.trade: Lacks a little reactivity and length, and struggles to finish smashes.
reviews.compared: Nox AT10 Genius 12K 2025, Nox AT10 Genius 12K Light 2026, Nox EA10 Ventus Attack 12K 2026

reviews.creator: Simone Mazzola Padel
reviews.quote: Impattati bene, vengono chirurgici, eh, impattati male decisamente meno.
reviews.summary: Plays the signature racket of Edu Alonso over several matches and a lesson, after a first game they call a near disaster. Finds the sweet spot not generous, with output that changes a lot when the ball is hit off centre, especially on lobs. Praises the rough surface for spin on volleys, bandejas and the worked vibora, and rates the chiquita and offensive transition very highly. Calls it not a cannon but unusually powerful for a heavy, hard racket. Notes the hard feel can be felt on the arm and the full-arm vibora is less agile. Rates it 8.05 overall and says it needs an advanced level and patience.
reviews.more: Removes the custom grip and uses an overgrip, since the handle underneath is very thin and hard to play without one. Finds the lob the trickiest shot, going deep when hit well but short without leg drive or off the sweet spot. Suggests it for a right-side player who likes to attack, or a left-side player who builds the point. Adds that a thermal cover comes with it, which they value.
highlights: unusually powerful for a heavy, hard racket
needs an advanced level and patience

reviews.trade: Small sweet spot and a tough first match; not for intermediate players.

reviews.creator: Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel
reviews.quote: Es la más controlable del trío.
reviews.summary: Tests it against the Nox AT10 12K and AT10 18K, playing all three on the same day. Weighs 369 g on their unit, with balance around 25.7 cm, and finds it the stiffest, driest and least bouncy of the three. Rates it the most controllable in volleys and for speed management, with a stable feel. Finds power harder to extract in smashes, needing harder and more precise hits. Advises players with elbow or arm pain to pick one of the other two. Sees the sweet spot as pleasant in the centre but smaller on the bandeja. Calls it useful for players who find the other two too bouncy.
reviews.more: Explains that the white AT10 12K uses a more reactive HR3 Black Eva, while the AT10 18K and this racket share the MLD rubber. Orders reactivity as AT10 12K, then AT10 18K, then this one. Finds volleys safer but prone to landing short without a longer swing. Thinks it may smash better in hot weather with new balls. Sees the AT10 18K and the aluminised AT10 12K as easier to lift on smashes, thanks to more flexible faces.
highlights: Finds power harder to extract in smashes
reviews.short: Tests it against the Nox AT10 12K and AT10 18K, playing all three on the same day. reviews.keyPoint: Firm, dry and controllable, but demanding on smashes.
reviews.stood: Most controllable in volleys and speed management of the three.
reviews.trade: Needs more technique and effort for power, and is harder on the arm.

reviews.creator: Probando Palas
reviews.quote: esta EA10 es una pala super polivalente
reviews.summary: Tests it from the baseline, at the net and on overheads, with a unit weighing 366 g and a 260 mm balance. Finds a medium-hard, dry feel that gives good ball exit at medium pace and works even better at high pace. Rates maneuverability and control highly, and says the double rough surface adds grip and spin. Calls the sweet spot average for a hybrid shape. Notes the medium balance means a longer swing on the bandeja, while smashes and accelerated volleys perform above average. Expects to place it among the most versatile rackets of 2026.
reviews.more: Compares the feel to the 2025 AT10 12K, calling it very similar. Finds the 2026 rough surface better optimised than the previous year's, which slipped a little on the AT10. Likes the two-density MLD rubber with 12K carbon, saying it gives some ball exit at medium pace without swallowing the ball at high pace. Wants to see how the rough surface lasts over time. Says the racket is not very demanding on balance and suits accelerating play.
highlights: good ball exit at medium pace
double rough surface adds grip and spin
smashes and accelerated volleys perform above average

reviews.stood: Surprisingly good volleys and accelerated play, with a grippy rough surface.
reviews.trade: Sweet spot only average and overheads need a longer swing.

reviews.creator: Dani 13
reviews.quote: es como una Nox de 13 un pelín más dura
reviews.summary: Tests it on court in four zones, with two overgrips over the wood and a weight of 362 g without string. Finds good handling with a medium balance, though slightly less nimble than the AT10 12K Extreme. Rates control as the main strength, especially when attacking firmly, since the ball does not fly easily to the glass. Notes a standard sweet spot that becomes drier when hitting high toward the edges on víbora and bandeja. Calls the smash potent for its handling, with a little more response than the Nox D13. Suits players with medium to good technique who want a dry feel.
reviews.more: Compares it with the AT10 12K Extreme, which gives more help in smashes and moves slightly better, while this one rebounds less and feels drier. Finds the volley zone the best part, with confidence to hit firmly. Notes slow rhythms ask for more pushing than other Nox rackets. Calls it a slightly harder Nox D13 and groups it with attacking hybrids such as the Oxdog Hyper Pro, Hack Hybrid and Combat Fuji. Picks it as the best Nox this year for players wanting a dry feel.
highlights: good handling with a medium balance

reviews.creator: Padel Review
reviews.quote: Da fondo campo è controllo totale.
reviews.summary: Tests it on court with a second player, covering baseline, lob, net and overhead play, then scores each area. Finds total control from the baseline, a hard feel and a homogeneous face, but a sweet spot that is decent rather than large. Reports that lobs often land short and the net game took until the third match to grasp. Calls it very manoeuvrable at 364 g with a centre balance, and more powerful on the smash than expected for its specs. Rates control and manoeuvrability 9 out of 10, power 8 and value 6. Suits an upper intermediate player who builds points and does not need a cannon.
reviews.more: Advises giving it time, since it does not give much away and stays short when the player is tired. Describes it as a construction racket rather than a finishing one, suited to placing the ball and being incisive only at chosen moments. Notes the lack of a weight balance system, so no added weights. Finds it good at fast rhythm, on the flat smash and on the vibora, with plenty of spin. Warns not to expect a cannon. Mentions a more offensive blue version they hope to test.
highlights: more powerful on the smash than expected
reviews.short: Tests it on court with a second player, covering baseline, lob, net and overhead play, then scores each area. reviews.keyPoint: Total control from the baseline, but demanding at the net.
reviews.stood: Total control and agility from the baseline, with a surprisingly good smash.
reviews.trade: Lobs land short, net play takes time to learn, and it is pricey.

reviews.creator: Mejora Tu Padel
reviews.quote: mucho control a baja velocidad y que hace fácil lo difícil
reviews.summary: Tests it in a five-way comparison of 2026 hybrid rackets, after playing with it a lot, including on a trip to Rotterdam. Describes a rough 12K carbon face and a medium hardness Black EVA core. Finds it very manoeuvrable, with the sweet spot close to the hand and a lot of control at low speed. Misses some power and balance on overhead shots compared with its sister model, which gives more leverage. Finds volleys a little short with it. Rates it as very easy to use, but prefers two other rackets with more hardness and balance.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Nox AT10 12K, which has a slightly harder Black EVA core, though both are medium hardness in the range. Notes the sister model gives more leverage, while this one keeps the sweet spot very close to the hand. Prefers two other rackets from the comparison, which have notably more hardness, a little more balance and a drier ball feel. Still calls it very easy to use, with incredible control.
highlights: sweet spot close to the hand
a lot of control at low speed
reviews.short: Tests it in a five-way comparison of 2026 hybrid rackets, after playing with it a lot, including on a trip to Rotterdam. reviews.keyPoint: Very easy hybrid with great control at low speed.
reviews.stood: Easy to play, with a sweet spot near the hand and low speed control.
reviews.trade: Less power and balance on overheads, and volleys fall a little short.

reviews.creator: Peter Consuegra
reviews.quote: he encontrado una relación muy buena entre potencia y control
reviews.summary: Tests the teardrop shape on court in defence, volley, overhead play and smash. Finds a compact, firm feel where the ball leaves fast, and a racket that feels heavier than other teardrops but still easy to move. Rates the volley as outstanding and finds defence comfortable, with plenty of speed from the back. Notes less help on the viper, gaining control and losing some power overhead. Calls the smash by three and the forward smash good. Prefers the blue diamond racket for aerial play, yet recommends this one for upper intermediate players wanting a complete, powerful racket with plenty of control.
reviews.more: Describes a red finish, dual spin rough surface, full carbon frame and no weight opening, unlike other models in the range. Notes the MLD Black EVA rubber is multilayer and comfortable, and less powerful than HR3 rubber, though the HR3 felt slightly harder on court. Expects the 12K Xtreme face to be firmer than the aluminised version, but notices no substantial difference. Links the extra power usually to the AT10 12K, and says the Tapia model feels closer to the 18K, with a less hard touch.
highlights: gaining control and losing some power overhead
reviews.short: Tests the teardrop shape on court in defence, volley, overhead play and smash. reviews.keyPoint: Compact teardrop that mixes control with extra power.
reviews.stood: Very good balance of power and control, especially at the net.
reviews.trade: Less help on the viper, so overhead power is limited.
reviews.compared: Nox AT10 Genius 12K, Nox AT10 Genius 18K

reviews.creator: el4Set
reviews.summary: Tests the Hybrid against the Attack with Edu Alonso in a 40-ball control challenge and a smash distance test. Finds the Hybrid gives a bit more control and maneuverability, with a low balance that makes defence easy, while the Attack sends the ball further when hit on the sweet spot. Measures the balance at 25 cm in their own setup, without string and factory grip and with two overgrips. Describes a medium-high ball output and intermediate hardness, shared with the Attack. Recommends it for players who want a control racket with low balance and comfortable defence.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Attack, which has a handle 1 cm longer at 13 cm and feels heavier in the head. Finds the Attack gives more power for fast courts but loses some control. Notes both use 12K Extreme carbon and MLD Blackba double-density rubber, the same rubber as last year's AT10. Says the new AT10 12K Alum Extreme feels stiffer and drier. Adds that the two differ only in mould and handle size, and that Edu Alonso picked the Hybrid for slow courts.
highlights: a bit more control and maneuverability
low balance that makes defence easy

reviews.stood: More control and maneuverability than the Attack, easy to defend with.
reviews.trade: Less power than the Attack, which may lack punch on fast courts.
reviews.compared: Nox EA10 Attack, Nox AT10 12K Alum Extreme

reviews.creator: PADEL WORLD
reviews.quote: it's got a textured surface which feels very nice
reviews.summary: Asks a coach who has played the Endure V1 for a while for thoughts after a friendly match. Likes the textured, grippy surface, the laminated edge and the stiff profile, and says the yoke gives torsional stability so the frame does not twist. Calls 365 g a great weight and says it feels nice to hold. Rates it as a good first advanced racket for a player who already knows they like padel, and not an intro racket. Says a lighter version keeps the same texture, edge support and yoke. Likes the shape and design too.
reviews.more: Points players still unsure about padel to a softer, more forgiving Head entry-level racket with a big sweet spot instead. Explains that beginner rackets are thin and can break, so the laminated circumference of the Endure helps a player moving up. Says the profile goes thin and wider, and the width gives stiffness and then feel. Calls control foam the main thing. Calls the Endure V1 and its lighter version rackets of the year.
reviews.short: Asks a coach who has played the Endure V1 for a while for thoughts after a friendly match. Likes the textured, grippy surface, the laminated edge and the stiff profile, and says the yoke gives torsional stability so the frame does not twist. Says a lighter version keeps the same texture, edge support and yoke. Likes the shape and design too.
reviews.keyPoint: Stiff, grippy racket for a first advanced step up.
reviews.stood: Textured grippy surface, stiff laminated edge and a comfortable 365 g weight.
reviews.trade: Not an intro racket, so not for players still unsure about padel.

reviews.creator: OngoalSweden
reviews.quote: Du har farten när du vill ha det.
reviews.summary: Tests the V1 next to the Pro and the lighter LS in a session of volleys, glass play and overheads, treating it as the reference model. Finds good pace and response when pushing, with a low balance that makes it easy to maneuver in fast volleys and quick strokes near the glass. Rates it softer than the Pro, which they put at about 10 percent stiffer, so the ball is felt more while stability and balance stay the same. Calls it a complete round racket for a broad group of hybrid players who want speed, control and balance.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Pro, which feels slightly stiffer and harder but not hugely different, and with the LS, which is 10 g lighter and softer and made one player work harder in defense. Describes it as a hybrid between the old Pro Staff and the Blade, with more feel than the Blade. Says the racket dampens the ball, which helps players who want to control tempo rather than only generate speed. Points to the Defy for players wanting the heaviest hitting Wilson.
highlights: easy to maneuver in fast volleys

reviews.keyPoint: Round racket that mixes pace with solid control.
reviews.stood: Low balance and good response in a round shape.
reviews.trade: Not the pick for players wanting maximum power.
reviews.compared: Wilson Endure Pro, Wilson Endure LS, Wilson Blade, Wilson Pro Staff, Wilson Defy

reviews.creator: Hotel Palas | La Suite del Padel
reviews.quote: Creo que es la pala más equilibrada en todas las zonas de pista.
reviews.summary: Tests the standard Endure against the Pro and LS in defence, volleys, bandeja and smash. Rates its hardness between medium and medium hard, with a dry feel that gives a direct contact and faithful ball speed. Finds control of the volleys very good with exact depth, though the balance is not high and it needs pushing forward. Calls handling average, perhaps because their sample weighed 371 g. Finds it the best mix of reactivity and sweet spot on bandeja, and only correct on smash, where it is more restrictive off the top of the face. Picks it as their favourite of the three and the most balanced across the court.
reviews.more: Compares it with the LS, which is softer, has more sweet spot and ball exit and handles better, but rebounds a little too much at times. Finds the Pro more precise on centre hits yet punishing high on the face, and the hardest to get power from. Notes the string cannot be swapped, the grip is longer at 13 cm, and a clear protector is included. Sees the three as suiting most players, provided control means speed control rather than softness.
highlights: dry feel that gives a direct contact
best mix of reactivity and sweet spot

reviews.keyPoint: Balanced control racket with a dry, direct feel.
reviews.stood: Best blend of reactivity and sweet spot, with very good volley control.
reviews.trade: Only correct on smashes, and less forgiving when hitting high on the face.
reviews.compared: Wilson Endure Pro, Wilson Endure LS

reviews.creator: Justpadel
reviews.quote: You can hold the racket lower actually feels nice.
reviews.summary: Reviews the 365 gram racket as a quick, precise option for the net, with fast reactions and a big sweet spot. Finds the multi-flex build sits between glass fiber and carbon, described as about 60% carbon feel and 40% glass fiber feel, with a soft control foam that still feels powerful at the net. Likes the thinner grip on the sides, which allows holding the racket lower, and calls the effect on the ball insane. Suggests it suits intermediate and pro level players who value control and precision in defense. Rates it 9.4 out of 10, but finds the smash can kick out for them, so would pick the Pro version for more power.
highlights: fast reactions and a big sweet spot
reviews.short: Reviews the 365 gram racket as a quick, precise option for the net, with fast reactions and a big sweet spot. reviews.keyPoint: Quick all round racket with a big sweet spot.
reviews.stood: Quick reactions at the net, big sweet spot and lots of effect.
reviews.trade: Smashes can kick out, so players wanting more power may prefer the Pro version.

reviews.creator: Extreme Padel
reviews.quote: The classic version retains very good precision and great control
reviews.summary: Tests the Endure Classic in a lab alongside the Pro and Light and Soft versions of the new round Wilson range. Notes a balance of 255 mm, slightly lower than the Pro, and a stiffness of 62 RA shared by the whole range. Describes a unidirectional carbon face with a less dense foam, which gives a drier feel at first but very few unwanted vibrations. Finds very good precision and great control. Calls the whole range easy to defend with. Recommends it to intermediate players at levels 4, 5 and 6 who want some precision while adding comfort.
reviews.more: Compares it with the Pro, which has a 257 mm balance, a 3K carbon face and the densest foam, and gives the best feel but demands the most physical effort. Notes the Light and Soft version weighs 355 g with a 260 mm balance and a fiberglass face, and is the most forgiving, suited to beginners. Mentions the Y-shaped bridge for stability and maneuverability, and a handle lengthened to 13 cm for two hands.
highlights: very good precision and great control
reviews.short: Tests the Endure Classic in a lab alongside the Pro and Light and Soft versions of the new round Wilson range. reviews.stood: Very good precision and great control with few unwanted vibrations.
reviews.trade: Feel is drier at first because of the unidirectional carbon face.
reviews.compared: Wilson Endure Pro, Wilson Endure Light and Soft

reviews.creator: Mejora Tu Padel
reviews.quote: ya se empieza a notar un poco más de cuerpo
reviews.summary: Tests the Endure range with a professional player, comparing the LS, V1 and Pro on defence and attack drills with target and off sweet spot tests. Describes the V1 as the standard version at 365 g with a low balance, 10 g heavier than the LS, with a drier, firmer feel. Finds it gives more body than the LS when missing the sweet spot, and the ball travels further forward. Rates it as more manoeuvrable than the Pro, with easier acceleration, drop shots and whip, but with less body. Notes the professional player chose the V1 for its overhead help, while they would pick the Pro.
reviews.more: Compares all three on the same drills: finds the LS loses direction off the sweet spot, while the Pro runs straighter and keeps inertia but accelerates worse. Calls the V1 the middle option for players wanting something neither too aggressive nor too soft. Says players who miss the centre often may prefer the Pro, while those who hit cleanly can get more from the V1.
highlights: easier acceleration, drop shots and whip
reviews.short: Tests the Endure range with a professional player, comparing the LS, V1 and Pro on defence and attack drills with target and off sweet spot tests. reviews.keyPoint: Balanced middle option that is easy to accelerate.
reviews.stood: More body than the LS, and easier to accelerate and manoeuvre than the Pro.
reviews.trade: Less body than the Pro, so it forgives off-centre hits less.
reviews.compared: Wilson Endure Pro, Wilson Endure LS

reviews.creator: Tino
reviews.quote: It makes returning the ball easy.
reviews.summary: Switches to the Motion after renting it and then buying it second-hand, and rates it 9/10. Puts it at around 360 grams, give or take 10, and finds it heavy but nice. Finds more pop and power than the Bullpadel Neuron 02, so low balls come back over the net without much effort. Notes the sweet spot is smaller, citing Padel Pro ratings of 8.0 against 9.2 for the Neuron 02, and maneuverability is worse. Limits sessions to two hours because of the weight. Suits beginners who play often and upper beginners, and advises complete newcomers to avoid it.
reviews.more: Advises against the Pro, calling it very heavy and too hard, and points to the Coello Team as a lighter option they have heard about. Suggests starting longer sessions with a lighter racket, then switching to the Motion in the second hour. Finds the extra power helps vibora, bandeja and overheads, and says it works for right-side and left-side players. Prefers dropping to a lighter racket over risking injury.
reviews.short: Switches to the Motion after renting it and then buying it second-hand, and rates it 9/10. Puts it at around 360 grams, give or take 10, and finds it heavy but nice. reviews.keyPoint: Powerful, heavy diamond racket best kept to two hours.
reviews.stood: More pop and power than a control racket, with easy returns of low balls.
reviews.trade: Heavy, with a smaller sweet spot, and only comfortable for about two hours.
reviews.compared: Bullpadel Neuron 02, Head Coello Pro, Head Coello Team

reviews.creator: Padel Smash TV
reviews.quote: This is definitely a balanced racket.
reviews.summary: Tests it on court alongside the heavier Coello Pro, describing it as the happy medium of the two. Lists 360 g, a diamond shape and a 268 mm balance, with a carbon hybrid surface and power foam feel. Finds the sweet spot a little higher, with the weight at the top. Calls it a good all around racket for the net, the base, defending and lobs. Finds it easy to control, putting the ball where intended even when slightly out of position. Expects most players to choose this over the Pro, a harder racket to use. Positions it for advanced players wanting power without a heavy frame.
reviews.short: Tests it on court alongside the heavier Coello Pro, describing it as the happy medium of the two. reviews.keyPoint: Balanced, easy to manage alternative to the heavier Pro.
reviews.stood: Well balanced and easy to control, even when slightly out of position.
reviews.trade: One reviewer still leans towards the heavier Pro for its power.

reviews.creator: Dani 13
reviews.quote: it is a racket that has given me better sensations than the Pro model
reviews.summary: Tests it for a few days in matches and training with newer and older balls, and compares it directly with the Coello Pro. Finds a wide sweet spot, good ball output and a hardness of around 6 out of 10, with a high balance that still asks for care in handling. Rates handling clearly better than the Pro, mainly at the net, and prefers it in defense, volleys and soft hits. Finds the power enough for attack, though the Pro gives more in the flat smash. Says it suits players wanting a more offensive racket without going too hard.
reviews.more: Places it near the Fenix Elite, with better handling and more sweet spot. Finds it less powerful than the Fenix Elite and a normal Metalbone, whose bounce is more exaggerated. Describes the feel as halfway between a Neuron 02 and a bouncier Adidas. Warns that arriving late leaves the tip behind and sends the ball too straight. Ranks the volley area first, then finishing, bandeja and defense.
highlights: handling clearly better than the Pro
more offensive racket without going too hard
reviews.short: Tests it for a few days in matches and training with newer and older balls, and compares it directly with the Coello Pro.
